case_name: Chandrakant Ganpat Sovitkar and another v State of Maharashtra
respondent:
State of Maharashtra
Supreme Court of India

3  May  1974
Cr.As. Nos. 206, 207 and 214 of 1970, Dt. 3 May 1974.
The Judgment was delivered by: JAGANMOHAN REDDY, J.
1.  These appeals are by special leave against the judgment of the Bombay High Court confirming the conviction and sentence passed on Rejendraprasad Devidas Mishra A-1 and Raghunandan Trivedi A-2 u/s. 161 read with Section 34, I.P.C. and S. 5(2) read with S. 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. A-1 was also convicted under Section 212, I.P.C. The two accused, along with Chandrakant Ganpat Sovitkar A-3, were tried for offences under Section 120-B, 161, 201, 212, 217, 218, I.P.C. and S. 5(2) read with S. 5(1)(d) of the prevention of Corruption Act, but A-3 was acquitted of all the charges and A-1 and A-2 were convicted and sentenced as aforesaid.
2. Further A-1 was also convicted by the Trial Court u/s. 218 I.P.C. but his conviction an sentence under that section was set aside
facts: The two accused, along with Chandrakant Ganpat Sovitkar A-3, were tried for offences under Section 120-B, 161, 201, 212, 217, 218, I.P.C. and S.5(2) read with S.5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
A-1 was also convicted under Section 212, I.P.C.
The prosecution case is that A-1 who was Inspector of Excise and A-2 who was Sub-Inspector of Excise were both posted at Indore.
They received certain information that Truck No. M.P.E. 5948 was carrying opium from Upper India to Hyderabad.
On receipt of this information the two accused left Indore on August 26, 1963 and reached Omerga via Hyderabad on September 3, 1963 with a view to intercept the said truck and seize the contraband.
issues: Whether there was a third person calling himself as K. Amar Singh in the station wagon MSW 7159 besides the drivers Sabir and Abrar responsible for the illegal possession and transport of the opium seized from the vehicle on 5-9-1963 at Omerga, and if so -
Which of the accused 1 to 3 knowingly and intentionally omitted to prosecute him ?
petitioner_arguments: The case of A-1 and A-2 is that there was no such person as K. Amar Singh and consequently there was no money as alleged by the prosecution.
respondent_arguments: The case of the prosecution was that A-1 had stated that K. Amar Singh was an informant and on that pretext his name was not deliberately shown nor was any mention made of the money.
court_reasoning: The main charge against the accused is that they accepted from K. Amar Singh large sum of money as illegal gratification to screen him from legal punishment for the offence of illegally possessing and transporting opium.

The receipt of money by the accused is, therefore, the main fact to be proved, of which it was admitted there is no direct evidence, either of the giver or of the accused being in possession of the money given as bribe.
holding: All the three accused were acquitted of this charge. They were also charged that they being public servants, accepted from the persons found with the Motor Vehicle No. MSW 7159 and calling himself as K. Amar Singh a large sum of about Rs. 40,000/- as gratification other than legal remuneration, as a motive or reward for forbearing to prosecute him for the offence of possessing and transporting opium and thereby committed an offence punishable u/s. 161 read with S. 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
cases_cited: should not disturb the finding of the trial Court, Bhim Singh v. State of Maharashtra
